In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cost of helium cryogenic systems is proportional to the total mass of the cryogenic system, and to the total power to be removed, and inversely proportional to the temperature of the system.
the cost of cryogenics is a function of the size of the system and of the temperature of operation, and that the cost per unit of power decreases as the size increases.
the cost of cryogenic systems for superconducting applications has been reduced by a factor 3 to 4 in 10 years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cost of cryogenic systems scales with the total refrigeration load and the number of cryogenic points, but not with the number of cryoplants or the total mass of cryogens.
the cost of a cryogenic system scales with its size, as expected, and that the performance of a system can be improved at a cost that is roughly proportional to its performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a large cryogenic system can be designed and constructed with an acceptable cost and risk if it follows the principles of good engineering practice, i.e. it should be modular, flexible and scalable, and it should be designed to be operated by non-specialists.

a significant cost reduction can be achieved by using the 1.8/4.5 K refrigeration scheme, and by optimising the design and performance of the cryogenic distribution system, which can be done by a proper sizing of the cold box.

the cost per unit of refrigeration power and per unit of cryogenic mass stored can be kept within reasonable limits, provided that the system is designed and operated in a way that maximises the efficiency of the cryogenic cycle and minimises the amount of equipment.
